Science.title: The Solar System chose fire over ice from the very beginning
Science.summary: Ancient iron meteorites reveal that some of the Solar System’s first solid bodies were built mostly from tiny heat-forged rock beads called chondrules, while water-rich dust was largely excluded. Science.title: Bennu asteroid samples point to a surprising origin involving Jupiter
Science.summary: The asteroid Bennu orbits the sun once every 1.2 years and approaches Earth every six years, passing within around 300,000 kilometers. NASA took advantage of this to collect material from the celestial body. In a spectacular operation in 2023, the US space agency collected samples from the surface of the asteroid Bennu by its OSIRIS-REx probe.

Science.title: One of America’s largest reservoirs just hit a record low
Science.summary: Lake Powell has fallen to its lowest level on record after an exceptionally dry and warm winter left the Colorado River Basin with little mountain snow to melt. Lake Mead also reached record lows, raising concerns for a river system that supplies water and power to more than 40 million people. Federal officials have taken emergency steps to stabilize Lake Powell, including sending in water from another reservoir and reducing releases downstream.

Science.title: Ancient genome function persists despite frequent mutations, centromere study shows
Science.summary: Every time a cell divides, its chromosomes must be distributed correctly between the two daughter cells. Central to this process is the centromere, a specialized region of the chromosome. The centromere serves as the attachment site for the cellular machinery that pulls the chromosomes apart.

Science.title: Weird spikes poking through a teen's eyelid turned out to be a wayward tooth

Science.title: Earth's first bats didn't come from where we thought, landmark genetic study reveals

Science.title: Evolved enzymes build tuberculosis antibiotic ingredient in the desired form, potentially reducing waste
Science.summary: Tuberculosis, or TB, is a contagious bacterial infection that primarily affects the lungs. While curative treatments exist, more than 80% of cases occur in low- and middle-income nations, where drug-resistant strains are on the rise and the cost of medications is a burden. A new class of antibiotics has shown promise against multidrug- and extensively drug-resistant TB, but its manufacturing cost is a barrier to access in poorer countries that need the treatments most.

Science.title: Combined satellite views offer clues to magma movement beneath Ethiopia's volcanoes
Science.summary: Magma moving beneath a volcano can make the ground rise, sink or shift sideways. Measuring these changes gives scientists clues about where magma is stored and how it travels. A study published in Geodesy and Geodynamics used satellite radar to examine the November 2025 eruption of Hayli Gubbi in Ethiopia's Afar Depression. Hayli Gubbi and nearby Erta Ale are separate volcanoes within the same volcanic zone, where three tectonic plates are pulling apart.

Science.title: Graphene measurements reveal energy-loss and quantum-coherence exponents diverge under gate control
Science.summary: Scientists have shown that the two exponents (inelastic scattering exponent and dephasing exponent) commonly used to describe electron scattering in graphene do not necessarily follow the same behavior. Using gated epitaxial graphene, a multi-institutional team of researchers independently extracted the two exponents through current-heating measurements and weak-localization analysis. The contrasting gate-voltage dependence provides evidence that energy relaxation and loss of quantum phase coherence can be governed by different microscopic processes.

Science.title: 'There was something bigger in the ground here': Metal detectorist in Germany discovers giant Roman-era hoard from time of emperor Hadrian

Science.title: Delaying cherry blossom to reduce frost damage
Science.summary: Climate change is causing many fruit trees to flower earlier, increasing their exposure to damaging late spring frosts. A study led by the University of Göttingen shows that the plant growth regulator ethephon can delay flowering in Kordia, a sweet cherry variety, potentially protecting blossoms and developing fruitlets from frost. The treatment did not significantly delay flowering in a second sweet cherry variety or two apple varieties, highlighting the importance of crop and cultivar selection. The results are published in BMC Plant Biology.

Science.title: Fluorescence timing identifies eight proteins in one cell with a single staining step
Science.summary: An international collaboration led by the University Medical Center Göttingen (UMG), Germany, has developed a labeling method that distinguishes fluorescent labels not by color but by how long it takes a dye to emit fluorescence. This makes it possible to visualize eight different proteins in a cell simultaneously in a single step using standard microscopes. The results have been published in the journal ACS Nano.

Science.title: Unevenness of global warming: Regional warming speedups emerge in waves

Science.title: Aiming at number 9: CASPAR targets fluorine in new science run
Science.summary: The Compact Accelerator System for Performing Astrophysical Research (CASPAR) recreates conditions inside stars to study how elements are made. The experiment recently restarted with a new target—the ninth element on the periodic table, fluorine.

Science.title: Central surface density of dark matter agrees with the prediction of a new theory of gravity

Science.title: How lawyers can better support clients living with dementia

Yet evidence shows that consumers are simultaneously exposed to complex mixtures of chemicals from many types of products.

Science.title: Starch-based sensor changes color to indicate moisture in food packaging

Science.summary: On Oct. 25, 2024, 10 days before the election that would return Republican Donald Trump to the White House and more than three months after Kamala Harris ascended to the top of the Democratic ticket, ChatGPT was still telling users that Joe Biden was running for a second term as president.

Science.title: Gene editing produces soybean with more than 90% oleic acid
Science.summary: Sejong University researchers have developed a high-quality soybean with improved oxidative stability, reduced saturated fat and increased seed fatty acid content. The research team led by Hyun Uk Kim, a professor in the Department of Bio-Industrial Resources Engineering at Sejong University, created the soybean line containing up to 90.2% oleic acid using CRISPR/Cas9 gene-editing technology. The study is published in the Plant Biotechnology Journal.

Science.title: The hunt for extraterrestrial life is fundamentally flawed. But there's a fix.
Science.summary: We search for aliens on exoplanets by looking for the chemical signatures of life. But without understanding the host star better, we may be misled says astrophysicist Alix Freckelton

Science.title: Fragment of world's oldest peace treaty unearthed in Turkey
Science.summary: Archaeologists excavating in the ancient Hittite capital of Hattusha have uncovered a fragment of the world's oldest peace treaty, signed around 1269 B.C.

Science.title: Astrophysicists use wave simulations to open a new window on dark matter
Science.summary: Astrophysicists from The University of Hong Kong (HKU), working with a research team led by Beijing Normal University (BNU), have developed a more physically realistic approach to testing how ultralight, or "fuzzy," dark matter could influence gravitationally lensed images. The study is the first to make gravitational-lensing predictions directly from three-dimensional wave simulations of fuzzy dark matter.

Science.title: 3,000-year-old burial of ancient Egyptian horse found — and a nearby stone carving depicts a captured prisoner
Science.summary: Archaeologists unearthed a horse burial dating back more than three millennia in an ancient Egyptian fortress.

Science.title: Banking patterns could help identify people experiencing financial abuse, UK study finds
Science.summary: Telltale signs of financial abuse, such as depleted savings, increasing debts and declining credit scores, can be identified in bank records, according to an analysis of U.K. banking data published in Nature. The findings reveal up to 373 indicators of financial behavior that could help pinpoint customers who may be experiencing economic abuse.

Science.title: Crown-of-thorns starfish can help reefs thrive
Science.summary: Crown-of-thorns starfish (COTS) are infamous in the marine world. Their toxin-loaded thorns give them a menacing appearance, and they have a reputation as destroyers of coral reefs. New research from the University of Sydney challenges the perception of COTS as purely destructive. The findings suggest controlled populations can have a positive impact on coral prevalence and diversity.

Science.title: Political shifts may shape how quickly Germany adopts electric cars and solar power
Science.summary: A new study conducted by the Climate Action Research Lab (CARL) at the University of Freiburg finds that electric cars and photovoltaic systems are less widespread on average in municipalities with strong support for Alternative for Germany (AfD). The researchers also examined how changes in political support within the same municipalities over time affect subsequent adoption of these technologies. Science.title: Cooling investments in apparel factories can pay for themselves, study shows
Science.summary: Investing in cooling for Bangladesh's apparel factories can be commercially viable, with an average payback period of one to four years, according to new research from Cornell University's Global Labor Institute (GLI).

Science.title: The LHC just ruled out another hiding place for quantum black holes
Science.summary: Physicists searching through Large Hadron Collider data found no evidence that the machine has been producing microscopic quantum black holes, but the result sharply narrows where such exotic physics could still be hiding. These hypothetical black holes could form if extra spatial dimensions make gravity much stronger at extremely tiny scales, potentially offering clues toward the long-sought theory of quantum gravity.

Science.title: GenAI use among online adult learners associated with academic performance and technology confidence
Science.summary: University of Phoenix scholars have published research examining how nontraditional undergraduate students use generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in online higher education. The study found that more frequent GenAI use was significantly associated with higher academic performance and stronger confidence in technology skills. Lower confidence in reading, writing and math, and greater time demands from work, study or family responsibilities, did not significantly predict use.

Science.title: Bee-made propolis boosts an antifungal drug against yeast pathogens in lab tests
Science.summary: Propolis may not only inhibit the growth of certain fungi but also affect the activity of drugs used to treat fungal infections. Researchers have investigated how an ethanolic extract of Polish propolis interacts with various antifungal agents.

Science.title: Do we live in a simulation? If so, it could be a giant consciousness experiment
Science.summary: Philosophers have pondered whether we live in a simulation for centuries. Now, Astronomer Royal for Scotland Catherine Heymans suggests a compelling rationale for why our reality might actually be synthetic

Science.title: Prefer intricate shapes? You may also favor complex melodies
Science.summary: A shape can be considered complex because it has many sides. A complex melody may feature varied pitches and rhythms. Does the mind treat these as separate features, or can it recognize something common beneath their differences?

Science.title: El Nino: Climate scientists warn of "Godzilla-level" climate event
Science.summary: Extreme heat caused by this year’s “super El Niño” could lead to as many as 451,000 excess deaths worldwide in the six months to February 2027, according to researchers at the University of Chicago’s Climate Impact Lab. The number of extremely hot days is expected to rise by 44%, with Nigeria, Indonesia and Sudan among the countries likely to be worst affected. Researchers warn that the impact could extend well beyond the six-month period studied. Carys Garland reports.

Science.title: Google DeepMind's latest AI tool promises a new era for genetics research, but experts warn to take its predictions with caution
Science.summary: AlphaGenome Atlas could make it easier for geneticists to access powerful AI, but its predictions aren't always accurate.

Science.title: Earth's crust is 'unzipping' beneath Italy — and that could explain most of the earthquakes in the region
Science.summary: The peeling away of Earth's crust beneath Italy may explain a lot of the seismic activity in the mountains that run along the spine of the country.
